title: Oath of innocence; wisdom beyond silver; buttered paths
english: … you have been stirred up to provoke me. I swear to you, and I swear by the living Lord himself, who judged that I should suffer these things, the very one who handed me over to these straits, who gave the devil authority to have me tested and tortured with such trials. I swear by the Lord, and I say: “The Lord lives, who has judged me thus, and the Almighty, who has embittered my soul” (Job 27:2).

“Far be it from me to declare you righteous until I die” (Job 27:5). If we were to agree with what you say, that you have understood why I have suffered these things, I would have declared you righteous until I die.
“For I will not put away my innocence” (Job 27:5). I will not stop giving heed to righteousness; I will remember always to hold fast to it.

“For I am not conscious of having done anything out of place” (Job 27:6). His freedom of speech is great, both about his earlier life and about what he did in the time of his trouble, so that he can say: “I am not conscious of having done anything out of place.”
“But what is the place of knowledge?” (Job 28:12). Knowledge is the grasp in contemplation of things that always stay the same; understanding is discernment.

“And silver will not be weighed out in exchange for it” (Job 28:15). Nothing is worth as much as wisdom. If you take the silver and the gold in the simpler sense, Job will at once be saying that nothing is worthy of wisdom.
“With precious onyx and sapphire” (Job 28:16). Wisdom will not be compared even with precious onyx; no, nor will it be made equal to a sapphire.

“Lofty things and gabis will not be mentioned” (Job 28:18). Neither lofty things nor gabis are worthy of wisdom. It seems to be set down of things that are mighty, as it were [gigantic]. But some say that “gabis” is the name for what stands up above the rim of a medimnus, which is called the heaped measure.

“And draw wisdom above the innermost things” (Job 28:18). The innermost things are those around India, or those in the country beyond it, where precious stones are found. That country yields these things to people, and among the rich they are thought marvellous. So beyond those innermost things, draw wisdom into yourself. Or else, “above the innermost things”: the holy mysteries of God within, which are beyond all telling. Above all things, many as they are, draw wisdom.
“It has escaped every human being” (Job 28:21). It has escaped every human being, even if he is a prophet, even if he is an apostle.

“When my paths were flowing with butter” (Job 29:6). We have said before about the paths Job walked, that they were virtues. So his paths flowed with butter: he walked in self-control, and his self-control flowed out, as it were, so that many, even of the little ones, were fed by Job's self-control, by Job's righteousness, by his courage. That is the meaning of “When my paths were flowing with butter.”
“And my mountains were flowing with milk” (Job 29:6). Whatever thoughts were high and great, these were Job's mountains, and he climbed up onto them.
“When I went out upright in the city” (Job 29:7). He gave his time to teaching and to doing good, out of love: not as a lover of himself, but as one who had a love that seeks the common good.

“Laying a finger on their mouth” (Job 29:9). It will seem that “laying a finger on their mouth” is a sign of silence. But perhaps, since the hand is taken for works, as we have often shown, it shows that they laid their work on their mouth: they perceived, being slight in work, that they were not worthy to speak while Job was present, who had done greater works.
“And those who heard me called me blessed” (Job 29:10).

From the same: So great was he, when he was not yet being tormented, that those who heard him called him blessed and wondered how he could understand and grasp so many things and was able to help those who heard him.
“For their tongue stuck to their throat” (Job 29:10). The tongue of those who heard me, and who called me blessed for what I said, stuck to their throat.
“For the ear heard and called me blessed” (Job 29:11).

From the same: It is written of Moses that he was afraid to look upon God because of the surpassing greatness of his brightness (Exodus 3:6). In the same way one might understand that Job's progress in wisdom was so surpassing that those who heard him could not look into the brilliance of his thoughts; and because they could not, they turned their eyes aside, unable to follow the great depth of his mind. That is why he says: “But the eye that saw me turned aside” (Job 29:11). Aquila and Symmachus have rendered it “It bore witness about me”; others, “But the eye that saw turned aside,” meaning: I am not strong enough to speak against him.

“For I rescued a poor man from the hand of the powerful” (Job 29:12). Let us look at his brave deeds and unfold them. This saying has a meaning according to the letter, and by way of anagogy it has an interpretation much more. According to the …

title: Foot to the lame; Elihu womb of words; night watches
english: … letter, we ought, as far as our strength allows, to help the poor who are oppressed by the powerful.
“And a foot to the lame” (Job 29:15). He himself gave steps even to those who were lamed, feet for the soul; and by his word he himself became their foot.
“And a cause I did not know, I searched out” (Job 29:16). He teaches us how we ought to judge, if we are ever called to arbitrate between brothers, so as to settle their affairs.

“And Job ceased from his words” (Job 31:40). “And his three friends also held their peace and no longer answered Job, for Job was righteous before them” (Job 32:1). He did not simply cease. His heart, which understood divine things, did not cease. For there is a time for every matter under heaven (Ecclesiastes 3:1): “a time to keep silent and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7). So when it was the time to answer the three, he spoke; when it was the time, after he had stopped their mouths, he fell silent. And I think the words “Job ceased” are said in his praise.

“Therefore I held my peace, afraid to declare my own knowledge to you” (Job 32:6). He has knowledge of how human beings suffer, of why human beings fall into certain straits if one looks at this life alone, and of how many prosper though they are unjust. I saw people doing wrong and breaking the law, and my feet were almost shaken. If I look into this life alone, my steps were all but poured away (Psalm 73:2).

“It is not the long-lived who are wise” (Job 32:9). For it does not follow, he says, that only old men are wise; it is possible to hear something noble from youth too. For if time makes people wise, God does so much more.

“For the spirit of my belly is destroying me” (Job 32:18). Just as a woman becomes pregnant, and when the child being born in her has been formed, she comes to her labor pains until she gives birth to what she had conceived before: think with me that something of this kind happens in the soul of the one who loves learning too. It conceives the word, and as it is being declared it shapes it and stamps it with order. And when, after stamping and shaping it, the word has become ready, it hands it over not as an unready and unfinished miscarriage, but, I would say, as something brought to term and made complete.

“And my belly is like a skin of new wine, fermenting and tied up” (Job 32:19). It seems to me that the saying in the Gospel was spoken from this place: “No one puts new wine into old wineskins” (Mark 2:22).

“I will speak so that I may find rest, when I have opened my lips” (Job 32:20). A man who meets with an understanding hearer, and is full of words, finds rest in speaking, and says: “I will speak so that I may find rest.”

“For I do not know how to admire a face” (Job 32:22). I do not have this skill, of admiring a person's face. No, I despise human beings, and the shame that mortals can bring, and the respect that they command.
“Otherwise the moths will devour me too” (Job 32:22). As though the moths eat through those who show partiality to the faces of men.

“If you have sinned, what will you do?” (Job 35:6). If you look up to heaven and consider the clouds, you will understand how you have sinned. What must you do? Come to the high priest and beg the high priest to offer a sacrifice for you. For “if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1-2).

“And if you have done much lawlessness, what can you do?” (Job 35:6). You will do this great thing: you will undo your many lawless deeds. That is why, for the incurable ills that we cannot heal in ourselves, Jesus Christ came from heaven, so that he might heal what is incurable and the word might come true: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered” (Psalm 32:1).

“Well then, since you are righteous, what will you give him?” (Job 35:7). But if you are righteous before God, what do you have to give in keeping with your righteousness? And if you are righteous, as you say, what will you add to him?

“He who appoints the night watches” (Job 35:10). He goes through the praises of God, his commendations and his hymns. The one who appoints the night watches is God himself. I want to see how God is the one who appoints the night watches. This whole age is night; it is darkness. The light is being kept for you. The light you see now, you see through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12). And “in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 36:9): one day we are going to see it. So the whole age is night; and since it is night, there are many wars, and many wild beasts prowl about.

“He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth” (Job 35:11). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth. For “man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them” (Psalm 49:20). If you are a sinner, you have not been separated from the four-footed beasts of the earth; rather, it is said to you: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 32:9). title: Gird like a man; do not reject my judgment; beasts beside you
english: … a little later: If you are a sinner, if you are a fornicator, if you are given to lust, you will not be separated from the four-footed beasts. “They became horses mad for mares” (Jeremiah 5:8). That is why he says with confidence that he has been set apart: “He who separates me from the four-footed beasts of the earth” (Job 35:11).

“No; but gird your loins like a man” (Job 40:7). I give you freedom of speech: I will ask you, and you answer me. God is already giving him a prize. He questions a man, in that he inquires of him, in that he gives him the right to answer. Had he not conquered, he would not have received this; had he not endured, he would not have heard: “Gird your loins like a man; I will ask you, and you answer me.”

From the same: Let no one answer God before he has become a man and girded his loins like a man. For as long as his loins are not girded, but slack, not bound round or drawn tight, he cannot fittingly answer the Lord.

“I will ask you, and you answer me” (Job 40:7). The full rewards of the contests are stored up, after this life, for those who have fought well. Yet even now, no less, the grace of God gives the athletes a pledge. That is why, when Job had fought the greatest fights; when he had lost his possessions and glorified the one who had given them; when he had put his children from him and given thanks to the one who had taken them; when he saw that he was, as it were, bringing up worms from his body and was not overcome by his pains: then God gives him the first-fruits and the pledge that belong to athletes, speaking to him through whirlwind and clouds. So when he had heard the earlier words, though he ought to have answered God, he keeps silent, as one who has no freedom to answer him. For he did not yet know what Moses wrote later, that “Moses spoke, and God answered him by a voice” (Exodus 19:19). Not knowing this, then, he does not want to answer God. But God gives him freedom to speak.

And after other matters: So great is the kindness of God that he takes on the role not of one who judges, but of one who goes to judgment with the man. And many Scriptures have taught this: “Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18). And: “My people” (or rather, God will argue his case with the people), “my people, what have I done to you, or how have I wearied you? Answer me” (Micah 6:3), and so on.

“Do not reject my judgment” (Job 40:8). Do not reject this judgment of mine. Let us keep this saying in mind as a useful one. Whenever God judges that we should suffer something, should lose a child, should lose a ruler, should fall ill in body, should endure any one of these things whatever: none of these can happen to us unless God judges it. For not even a sparrow falls into a snare without the will of the Father in heaven (Matthew 10:29). Since, then, none of these things happens apart from God's judgment, it is said to the one who suffers: “Do not reject my judgment”: do not deny that I have judged concerning you.

“Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” (Job 40:8). I am making my defense to you. You were righteous, but you were not seen to be. You had endurance; I had to give an occasion for your endurance to shine. You had courage, but it lay hidden in you; the toils that came upon you showed your courage.

And a little later: Let us remember these things in times of trouble, and let us think that we hear God present and saying to us: “Do you think I have dealt with you for any other reason than that you might be shown to be righteous?” Let us not be shown to be unrighteous, or ungodly.
“Take on, then, loftiness and power” (Job 40:10). Crown yourself; clothe yourself with glory, clothe yourself with honor.

“And send out angels in wrath, and humble every insolent one” (Job 40:11). “And quench the proud” (Job 40:12). The insolent one made war against you. The insolent one once said to me: “Put forth your hand.” He said to me: “Touch all that he has.” He said to me about you that you would surely bless me to my face (Job 1:11). But you have conquered all the same. That is why I say to you: Take courage; humble every insolent one, and humble his angels. That one became proud against you; but you, quench the proud. That one is ungodly against you; but you, strike down the ungodly at once.
“And fill their faces with dishonor” (Job 40:13). Convict sinners by showing them to be sinners. Fill their faces with dishonor through the conviction that is in you.

“But look, there are wild beasts beside you; it eats grass like oxen” (Job 40:15). The wild beasts are the opposing powers, about which the Prophet prayed, saying: “Do not hand over to the wild beasts the soul that confesses to you” (Psalm 74:19). The wild beasts are the opposing powers over which you, O man, have received authority. If you serve God, upon the asp …
